title: Ramps by Design
bigQuestion: How can the shape of a curve be chosen with physics so a ramp is fun, safe and right for the people who ride it?

story.title: Two Curves on the Table
story.kicker: A youth club must choose between two ramp plans that look almost the same from above.
paragraphs: On a folding table in a community center, two ramp plans lie side by side. Both are mini ramps 1.2 meters tall. Both have a flat stretch in the middle and a platform at each end. A volunteer named Teresa, who has built ramps for years, has drawn both. She asks the club's teenagers to pick one.

The first plan has a tight curve. Its transition is drawn from a circle with a radius of 1.5 meters. The ramp is short and fits easily in the small lot behind the building. The second plan uses a wide curve with a radius of 2.5 meters. It is longer, needs more plywood and stretches nearly to the fence.

A skater named Jalen likes the tight curve. "It looks steeper," he says. "More exciting." A younger rider named Ana frowns. She has felt a tight ramp before. "At the bottom it squishes you," she says. "Your knees fold if you are not ready." Teresa smiles and takes out a calculator.

"Ana felt something real," she says. "We can measure it before we buy a single board." She writes two lines on the plan: the speed a rider will have at the bottom, and how heavy the rider will feel there. The numbers for the two curves are not the same. The group leans in to see why.
story.think: Without doing any math yet, which curve do you think will make riders feel heavier at the bottom, and why?

lessons.title: A Curve From a Circle
lessons.mainIdea: Most ramp transitions are arcs cut from a circle, and the circle's radius sets how tight or mellow the curve feels.
reading: A *transition* is the curved surface that joins flat ground to the wall of a ramp. Skaters often call it tranny, and riding ramps and bowls is called transition skating. The first transitions people skated were the curved walls of empty backyard swimming pools during the California drought of 1976 and 1977. Builders later copied those curves in wood and concrete.

Most ramp builders draw a transition as part of a circle. The *radius* is the distance from the circle's center to its edge. A quarterpipe uses one quarter of a circle or less. If the curve runs a full quarter, from flat to straight up, the ramp's height equals the radius. A circle with a 1.5 meter radius makes a curve that reaches vertical 1.5 meters off the ground.

A small radius makes a tight curve. The rider turns from flat to steep in a short distance. A large radius makes a wide, mellow curve. The rider turns more gradually and has more room to react. Two ramps of the same height can feel completely different because their radii differ.

A ramp does not have to reach vertical. A mini ramp often stops before the curve gets straight up, so its top edge is steep but still tilted. A vert ramp continues the curve to vertical and then adds a short straight-up section on top. Vert ramps are usually more than 3 meters tall and are for experienced riders.

words.d: the curved surface that joins flat ground to the wall of a ramp or bowl
the distance from the center of a circle to its edge; it sets how tight a transition is
a single ramp whose curve is part of a quarter circle
a tall ramp whose curve reaches straight up, with a vertical section on top

look.title: Drawing the Curve With String
look.text: Picture a sheet of plywood flat on the ground. A nail sits at one corner, off the edge of the ramp's footprint. A string 1.5 meters long is tied to the nail, with a pencil at the other end. Pulling the string tight, you swing the pencil in an arc across the plywood. That arc is the transition of a ramp with a 1.5 meter radius.
look.prompt: How would you change the string to draw a mellower curve?

check.q: What is a transition?
choices: the flat top platform of a ramp
the metal pipe on the edge
the curved surface between flat ground and the wall
the stairs next to a ramp
check.why: A transition is the curve that joins the flat ground to the wall.

check.q: A quarterpipe's curve runs a full quarter circle from flat to vertical. Its radius is 2 meters. How tall is the curve?
check.why: When the curve runs a full quarter to vertical, its height equals the radius, so 2 meters.

check.q: Which ramp has the tighter curve?
check.why: A smaller radius bends from flat to steep in a shorter distance, so 1.5 meters is tightest.

lessons.title: How Steep Is the Top?
lessons.mainIdea: If a ramp stops before vertical, geometry tells you how steep its top edge is and how long the curve runs along the ground.
reading: A curve cut from a circle rises slowly at first and then faster. The height reached after the curve turns through an angle θ is h = r(1 − cos θ). Here r is the radius and θ is measured from flat ground. At θ = 90 degrees, cos θ is 0, so the height is the full radius. That is a vertical wall.

Here is a worked example. A builder wants a ramp 1.2 meters tall using a radius of 1.8 meters. First, divide: 1.2 ÷ 1.8 = 0.667. Next, solve 1 − cos θ = 0.667, so cos θ = 0.333. Then find the angle whose cosine is 0.333, which is about 70.5 degrees. The top edge of this ramp tilts at about 70 degrees from flat, steep but not vertical.

The same circle tells how long the curve runs along the ground. The horizontal length is r × sin θ. For this ramp it is 1.8 × sin 70.5° = 1.8 × 0.943 = 1.70 meters. The builder now knows that each side of the ramp needs about 1.7 meters of floor space for the curve alone, before adding any flat bottom or platform.

These two numbers, the top angle and the floor length, guide most design choices. A larger radius at the same height gives a gentler top angle but a longer footprint. A smaller radius gives a steeper top in less space. Space, budget and the riders' skill decide which way to go.

words.d: the amount a line or surface turns, measured in degrees; flat is 0 and straight up is 90
the area of ground a ramp covers
a ratio from geometry that links an angle to the sides of a right triangle; used to find how high a curve rises

look.title: Top Angle of a 1.2 m Ramp
look.unit: degrees from flat at the top edge
look.cite: Worked example: cos θ = 1 − h ÷ r with h = 1.2 m
look.prompt: What happens to the top angle as the radius grows while the height stays 1.2 meters?

check.q: For a curve with radius r turning through angle θ, which formula gives its height?
check.why: The height of a circular arc after turning through θ is r(1 − cos θ).

check.q: A ramp is 1.2 m tall with a 2.4 m radius. What is cos θ at the top?
check.why: cos θ = 1 − 1.2 ÷ 2.4 = 1 − 0.5 = 0.5, which is 60 degrees.

check.q: Keeping the height the same, what does a larger radius do?
choices: makes the top gentler and the footprint longer
check.why: A larger radius bends less before reaching the set height, so the top is gentler and the curve runs longer.

lessons.title: Coping, Platform and Flat Bottom
lessons.mainIdea: The coping, the platform and the flat bottom each give riders something they need: a grinding edge, a safe place to start and time between walls.
reading: The *coping* is the edge at the top of a transition. On a wooden ramp it is usually a round steel pipe fixed so it sticks out just past the riding surface. In a concrete pool or bowl it is often a row of stone or concrete blocks, a reminder of the backyard pools where skaters first rode it. Coping gives the trucks a hard, smooth edge to grind and gives the rider a clear signal that the wall has ended.

Behind the coping sits the *platform*, a flat deck where riders stand, wait their turn and start runs. A platform needs room to stand with a board and to step back safely. On taller ramps, a guardrail along the back keeps people from stepping off the edge. Riders set the tail on the coping here before dropping in.

The *flat bottom* is the level stretch between two transitions on a halfpipe. Without it, a rider would go from one curve straight into the next. A flat bottom gives a moment to settle, shift the feet and get ready for the next wall. Ignoring friction, it does not change the rider's speed, because a level surface neither raises nor lowers them. It does add length, cost and time.

A mini ramp for a youth club might have a flat bottom a few meters long. Too short and the walls come too fast. Too long and riders lose speed to friction before reaching the other side. Builders choose a length that fits the riders and the space, then mark it on the plan before cutting any wood.

words.d: the edge at the top of a transition, often a steel pipe or stone blocks, used for grinds
the flat deck at the top of a ramp where riders stand and start runs
the level stretch between two transitions on a halfpipe

look.title: A Halfpipe From the Side
look.text: Picture a halfpipe drawn from the side. On the left is a platform with a guardrail, then a steel pipe at the edge, then a curve sweeping down. In the middle is a level stretch. Then a matching curve sweeps up on the right to another pipe and another platform.
look.prompt: Name each part from left to right and say what each one does for the rider.

check.q: What is the coping on a wooden ramp usually made of?
check.why: Wooden ramps usually have a steel pipe at the top edge for the coping.

check.q: Ignoring friction, what does a flat bottom do to a rider's speed?
choices: it does not change the speed
it makes the rider go faster each time
check.why: A level surface neither raises nor lowers the rider, so with no friction the speed stays the same.

check.q: Why do taller ramps have a guardrail on the platform?
choices: to keep people from stepping off the back edge
to hold the coping in place
check.why: A guardrail along the back keeps people from falling off a high platform.

lessons.title: Height Becomes Speed
lessons.mainIdea: As a rider drops down a transition, potential energy turns into kinetic energy, so the drop height predicts the speed at the bottom.
reading: A rider standing at the coping of a 1.2 meter ramp has stored energy because of height. This is *potential energy*, equal to mgh: mass times g times height. For a 60 kilogram rider, it is 60 × 9.8 × 1.2 = 705.6 joules. A joule is the SI unit of energy, about the energy needed to lift a small apple one meter.

As the rider drops in, height turns into motion. Motion energy is *kinetic energy*, equal to ½mv². If no energy were lost, all 705.6 joules would become kinetic energy at the bottom. Setting mgh = ½mv² and cancelling the mass gives v = √(2gh). The mass cancels, so a light rider and a heavy rider reach the same speed in this ideal case.

Work it through. With h = 1.2 m, v = √(2 × 9.8 × 1.2) = √23.52 = 4.85 meters per second. That is about 17 kilometers per hour. The shape of the curve does not change this answer. A tight curve and a wide curve of the same height give the same ideal speed at the bottom, because only the height drop counts.

The same idea runs backward. A rider moving at 4.85 meters per second at the bottom can, with no losses, coast up to 1.2 meters on the other wall. The rule of *conservation of energy* says energy is not created or destroyed; it changes form. This is why a rider rolling back and forth can predict how high each wall will carry them.

words.d: stored energy from height, equal to mass × g × height (mgh)
energy of motion, equal to one half × mass × speed squared
the rule that energy is not created or destroyed, only changed in form

look.title: Ideal Speed at the Bottom
look.cite: Worked example: v = √(2gh) with g = 9.8 m/s², no friction
look.prompt: The drop goes from 0.5 m to 2.0 m, four times as high. Does the speed also become four times as fast?

check.q: A 50 kg rider stands at the top of a 1.0 m ramp. What is the potential energy?
Why do a light rider and a heavy rider reach the same ideal speed at the bottom?
choices: the mass cancels out of mgh = ½mv²
the ramp gets steeper for heavy riders
check.why: Mass appears on both sides of mgh = ½mv², so it cancels and v = √(2gh).

check.q: Two ramps are the same height but one has a tighter curve. With no friction, which gives more speed at the bottom?
choices: it depends on the rider's mass
check.why: Only the drop height sets the ideal speed, so both curves give the same speed.

lessons.title: Losses and Pumping
lessons.mainIdea: Friction and air drain energy on every pass, and riders replace it by pumping: crouching high and pressing up through the bottom of the curve.
reading: In real life a rider never quite reaches the starting height on the next wall. Rolling resistance in the wheels, friction in the bearings and air pushing on the body turn some energy into heat. Suppose a 60 kilogram rider drops from 1.2 meters and coasts up only 1.0 meter on the other side. The energy lost is mg times the difference: 60 × 9.8 × 0.2 = 117.6 joules, about one sixth of the 705.6 joules they started with.

Riders make up for the loss without pushing off the ground. They *pump*. First, the rider stays low in a crouch as the board rolls down from the top of the wall. Next, as the board passes through the bottom of the curve, the rider presses up through the legs and stands taller. Then they crouch again near the top of the next wall. Done well, each pass climbs a little higher.

Pumping works because the rider pushes hardest where the ramp pushes back hardest. At the bottom of the curve the board presses up with extra force, so standing up there takes more work than it gives back when the rider crouches near the top, where the push is weaker. The extra work becomes extra energy. A child on a swing adds energy in a similar way by moving their body at the right moments.

A common problem is pumping on the flat bottom instead of the curve. Standing up on flat ground adds nothing, because the floor pushes back only with normal body weight. Another problem is leaning back on the wall, which makes the board shoot out. The fix is to keep the shoulders over the board, square to the ramp surface, and to save the push for the curve.

words.d: to gain speed on a ramp by crouching and then pressing up through the legs at the bottom of the curve
the drag that slows a rolling wheel as it squashes against the ground
the SI unit of energy

look.title: One Pump, Step by Step
look.text: Picture a rider rolling down from the coping, knees bent, arms loose. As the board sweeps through the lowest part of the curve, the rider straightens the legs, pressing the board down into the ramp. Rolling up the next wall, they bend the knees again. The board climbs a few centimeters higher than on the last pass.
look.prompt: Where exactly in the ramp should the rider press up, and what happens if they press too early on the flat?

check.q: A 60 kg rider drops from 1.0 m and only reaches 0.8 m on the next wall. How much energy was lost?
check.why: Energy lost = mg × height difference = 60 × 9.8 × 0.2 = 117.6, about 118 joules.

check.q: When does a rider press up through the legs to pump?
choices: while standing still on the platform
in the middle of the flat bottom
at the very top of the coping
as the board passes through the bottom of the curve
check.why: Pumping works by pressing up where the ramp pushes back hardest, at the bottom of the curve.

check.q: A rider keeps leaning back on the wall and the board shoots out. What helps?
choices: keeping the shoulders over the board, square to the ramp
standing straight up on the coping
check.why: Staying square to the ramp surface keeps the weight over the board so it does not shoot out.

lessons.title: Dropping In With Energy in Mind
lessons.mainIdea: Dropping in turns a standing rider's height into speed, and committing the front foot keeps the board under the body.
reading: Dropping in means starting a run from the top of a ramp instead of rolling in from the flat. It is the moment when the most potential energy turns into motion. Learn it on a small ramp, with a helmet that fits and is buckled, wrist guards and knee pads, and with a friend or coach nearby. Many learners first practice by rolling up a ramp and riding back down fakie, so they know the feel of the curve.

First, set the tail on the coping with the back wheels hooked behind it and the back foot on the tail. Next, put the front foot over the front bolts. Then lean forward and press the front foot down firmly, so the front wheels touch the ramp and the body moves with the board. The board drops and rolls away, and the rider rides it down in a low, balanced crouch.

The physics explains the most common problem. If the rider leans back, the board accelerates down the slope but the body stays behind at the top. The board shoots ahead and the rider falls backward. Committing the front foot keeps the body's center of mass over the board as both speed up together.

Falling small is part of learning. If a drop-in goes wrong, crouch low, let the knee pads touch first and slide down the transition on them. Do not reach back with locked straight arms, which is how many wrist injuries happen. Fear before a drop-in is a normal signal. Breaking the move into smaller steps, such as practicing on a lower ramp, helps it shrink.

words.d: to start a run from the coping at the top of a ramp
rolling backward while standing in your normal stance
the point where an object's mass is balanced; for a rider, near the hips

look.title: The Drop-In, Pictured
look.text: Picture a rider on a low ramp. The tail rests on the coping, back wheels hooked behind it, back foot on the tail. The front foot hovers over the front bolts. The rider leans forward and stamps the front foot down. Board and body tip together, and the rider rolls down in a crouch, eyes ahead.
look.prompt: Describe what would happen if the rider kept weight on the back foot instead.

check.q: Where does the back foot go to set up a drop-in?
choices: on the tail, with the tail on the coping
on the platform beside the board
check.why: The tail sits on the coping with the back foot on it; the front foot goes over the front bolts.

check.q: Why does leaning back cause a fall on a drop-in?
choices: the board slows down too much
the board speeds away while the body stays behind
check.why: The board accelerates down the slope while the body stays back, so the board shoots out.

check.q: What is the safer way to fall on a ramp?
choices: lean back and sit down hard
crouch low and slide down on the knee pads
check.why: Crouching and sliding on knee pads spreads the impact; straight arms often lead to wrist injuries.

lessons.title: Why Riders Feel Heavier
lessons.mainIdea: At the bottom of a curve, the ramp must push up extra hard to bend the rider's path, so the rider feels heavier.
reading: Anything moving in a circle is accelerating toward the circle's center, even at a steady speed, because its direction keeps changing. This is *centripetal acceleration*, and it equals v²/r: speed squared divided by the radius. At the bottom of a transition, the center of the circle is above the rider. So the ramp must push up harder than usual to curve their path upward.

The upward push of a surface is the *normal force*. On flat ground it equals body weight, mg. At the bottom of the curve, Newton's second law gives N − mg = mv²/r, so N = m(g + v²/r). The rider's legs feel that larger force. Riders sometimes describe it as the ramp squishing them, which is what Ana felt in the story.

Work it through for a 60 kilogram rider who drops in from 1.2 meters on a curve with a 2.0 meter radius. The speed at the bottom is 4.85 meters per second, so v² = 23.52. Then v²/r = 23.52 ÷ 2.0 = 11.76 m/s². The normal force is 60 × (9.8 + 11.76) = 60 × 21.56 = 1,293.6 newtons. Body weight is 60 × 9.8 = 588 newtons, so the rider feels about 2.2 times as heavy.

There is a shortcut. Because v² = 2gh after a drop from height h, the felt weight at the bottom is 1 + 2h ÷ r times normal. For the 1.2 meter drop on a 2.0 meter radius, that is 1 + 2.4 ÷ 2.0 = 2.2. If the drop height equals the radius, the rider feels three times as heavy. This simple model treats the rider as a point and ignores friction.

words.d: the acceleration toward the center of a curve, equal to speed squared ÷ radius (v²/r)
the push of a surface straight out from it, against whatever presses on it
the SI unit of force

look.title: Felt Weight After a 1.2 m Drop
look.cite: Worked example: felt weight = 1 + 2h ÷ r, h = 1.2 m, no friction
look.prompt: Which of Teresa's two plans, the 1.5 m or the 2.5 m radius, would make Ana's knees work harder?

check.q: What is the formula for centripetal acceleration?
check.why: Centripetal acceleration equals speed squared divided by the radius, v²/r.

check.q: A rider moves at 4 m/s at the bottom of a curve with a 2 m radius. What is the centripetal acceleration?
Why does a rider feel heavier at the bottom of a transition?
choices: the ramp must push up extra to curve the rider's path
check.why: The normal force must supply mg plus mv²/r to bend the path upward, so the legs feel more force.

lessons.title: Why Tight Curves Feel Harder
lessons.mainIdea: A tighter curve gives a bigger and more sudden jump in force and less time to react, so it demands more strength and skill.
reading: Look again at the shortcut: felt weight = 1 + 2h ÷ r. The height is fixed by the ramp, so a smaller radius makes the number larger. In Teresa's plans, both ramps are 1.2 meters tall. The 1.5 meter radius gives 1 + 2.4 ÷ 1.5 = 2.6 times body weight. The 2.5 meter radius gives 1 + 2.4 ÷ 2.5 = 1.96, about 2 times. The tight curve asks the legs to hold about 30 percent more force.

The force also arrives suddenly. On the flat bottom, a rider feels normal weight. The moment the wheels enter the curve, the felt weight jumps to its high value. Builders call a harsh jump like this a *kink*. A badly built ramp with a bump or flat spot where the curve meets the flat makes the kink worse. Smooth joints and a carefully drawn curve make the change feel gentler.

A tight curve also leaves less time. The rider covers the curve in a shorter distance, so there is less time to shift weight, bend the knees and stay square to the surface. Small errors grow fast. A mellow curve gives a learner more time to feel what is happening, which is why beginner ramps usually have wide transitions and low walls.

Tight curves are not wrong. Many experienced riders like them because they turn the board quickly and throw the rider up the wall. The point is fit. A ramp for a youth club with many beginners usually gets a wider radius. A ramp for advanced riders in a small space may use a tighter one.

words.d: a harsh, sudden change in a ramp's curve that riders feel as a jolt
skater word for a gentle, gradual curve or slope
how heavy a rider feels, set by the normal force pushing up on them

look.title: Ana and Jalen on Two Ramps
look.text: Picture Jalen on the tight 1.5 meter curve. He reaches the bottom, his legs suddenly hold 2.6 times his weight, and an instant later he is already climbing the wall. Now picture Ana on the 2.5 meter curve. The force builds to about 2 times her weight, and the wall arrives more slowly, giving her time to stay balanced.
look.prompt: Which ramp would you build for a club where most riders are learning to drop in, and what numbers support your choice?

check.q: Using felt weight = 1 + 2h ÷ r, what is the felt weight for h = 1.0 m and r = 2.0 m?
check.why: 1 + 2 × 1.0 ÷ 2.0 = 1 + 1 = 2.0 times body weight.

check.q: What is a kink on a ramp?
choices: a harsh, sudden change in the curve
check.why: A kink is an abrupt change in the curve that riders feel as a jolt.

check.q: Why do beginner ramps usually have wide transitions?
choices: they make the rider go faster
they give lower forces and more time to react
check.why: A larger radius lowers the felt weight and gives more time on the curve.

lessons.title: Ribs, Stringers and Plywood
lessons.mainIdea: A wooden ramp is a frame of curved ribs joined by stringers and covered with layers of thin plywood bent to the curve.
reading: Most wooden ramps share one structure. The sides are *ribs*, flat pieces of thick plywood cut to the shape of the transition. Builders draw the curve on the first rib with a string and pencil, cut it, and trace it to make matching ribs. Ribs are spaced along the width of the ramp, with extra ribs for wider ramps, so the surface never spans a long gap.

Between the ribs run *stringers*, pieces of framing lumber laid across the curve like rungs on a ladder. They sit close together, often every 20 to 30 centimeters, so the surface is supported at many points. Closer spacing is needed where the curve is steep and where riders land hardest, near the bottom.

The riding surface goes on in layers. Thin plywood bends to the curve without cracking, so builders screw down two or more thin layers, one over the other. They stagger the seams so the joints in one layer do not line up with the joints in the next. That keeps the surface from forming a ridge where sheets meet. A smooth top layer goes on last.

The coping is bolted along the top edge of the transition so it sits slightly proud, meaning it sticks out a little past the riding surface. The platform is framed like a small floor behind it. For an outdoor ramp, builders choose wood rated for weather, raise the frame off the ground and cover the ramp in rain, because wet plywood swells, warps and rots.

words.d: flat pieces of plywood cut to the shape of the transition that form a ramp's sides and frame
framing pieces that run across between ribs to support the riding surface
to place joints so they do not line up from one layer to the next

look.title: Building Order
look.text: Step 1: Draw the curve on plywood with a string and pencil, and cut the first rib. Step 2: Trace it to cut the matching ribs. Step 3: Stand the ribs up and screw stringers across them. Step 4: Screw down the first thin layer of plywood. Step 5: Add the second layer with seams staggered. Step 6: Add the top layer, the coping and the platform.
look.prompt: Why is it important that every rib is traced from the same first rib?

check.q: What are the ribs of a ramp?
choices: plywood pieces cut to the transition's shape
the steel pipe at the top
check.why: Ribs are plywood pieces cut to the curve; they form the ramp's frame.

check.q: Why do builders stagger the seams in the surface layers?
choices: so joints do not line up and form a ridge
check.why: Staggering keeps joints in one layer from lining up with joints below, so the surface stays smooth.

check.q: Why are stringers placed closer together near the bottom of the curve?
check.why: The bottom of the curve takes the largest forces, so it needs more support.

lessons.title: Building Safely
lessons.mainIdea: Safe ramp building means protecting the builders, choosing a good site and checking the finished ramp before every session.
reading: Building a ramp uses saws, drills and heavy sheets of wood. Young builders work with an experienced adult who runs the power tools or watches closely. Everyone wears safety glasses, and hearing protection when saws run. Gloves help when carrying plywood, but builders keep loose gloves and sleeves away from spinning blades. Cords are kept out of walkways so no one trips.

Pick the site before buying wood. A ramp needs firm, level ground, with clear space around it and nothing hard nearby for a rider to hit. It should be away from streets, driveways and parked cars. Many towns have rules about structures in yards or shared spaces, so builders ask the property owner and check local rules first.

Details on the surface matter. Every screw head is driven slightly below the surface so wheels and knee pads do not catch on it. Sheet edges are sanded smooth. The coping is bolted tight, and its ends are capped or rounded. The first ramp a group builds should be small, because a low ramp is easier to learn on and a fall from it is shorter.

A finished ramp still needs care. Before each session, someone walks the surface looking for loose screws, cracked sheets, soft spots and gaps at the seams. Rain and sun wear plywood down, so the ramp is covered when not in use. A damaged section is fixed before anyone rides it again.

words.d: protective eyewear worn when cutting, drilling or sanding
to drive a screw head slightly below the surface so nothing catches on it
a careful check of a ramp for damage before it is ridden

look.title: A Safety Agency on Skate Areas
look.text: Skaters should ride in places away from traffic, check the riding surface for holes, bumps, rocks and debris before riding, and wear a helmet and other protective gear.
look.cite: U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission, skateboarding safety guidance
look.prompt: Which of these ideas should a ramp crew add to its inspection before each session?

check.q: Why should every screw be countersunk?
choices: so the screws hold the coping
so wheels and knee pads do not catch on screw heads
check.why: Driving screws below the surface keeps heads from catching wheels or pads.

check.q: Which is the best site for a backyard ramp?
choices: firm, level ground away from streets
on a soft lawn near a fence
check.why: A ramp needs firm, level ground with clear space and no traffic.

check.q: What should happen before each riding session?
choices: inspect for loose screws, cracks and soft spots
check.why: A quick inspection catches damage before anyone rides on it.

lessons.title: A Worked Design Problem
lessons.mainIdea: Good ramp design puts the numbers together: height, radius, top angle, footprint, speed and felt weight, then checks them against the riders.
reading: Return to the youth club. The lot is 9 meters long. The club wants a mini ramp 1.2 meters tall for mostly beginner and intermediate riders. Teresa proposes a 1.8 meter radius. The lot also needs room to walk around the ramp. Here is the full check, step by step, using the formulas from the earlier lessons.

First, the top angle. cos θ = 1 − 1.2 ÷ 1.8 = 0.333, so θ is about 70.5 degrees: steep but not vertical. Second, the footprint of each curve. Its length is 1.8 × sin 70.5° = 1.8 × 0.943 = 1.70 meters. Third, the speed at the bottom. v = √(2 × 9.8 × 1.2) = √23.52 = 4.85 meters per second, ignoring losses.

Fourth, the felt weight at the bottom: 1 + 2 × 1.2 ÷ 1.8 = 1 + 1.33 = 2.33 times body weight. That sits between the tight plan's 2.6 and the wide plan's 1.96. Fifth, the total length. Two curves at 1.70 meters each make 3.40 meters. A flat bottom of 2.4 meters brings it to 5.80 meters. Two platforms of 1.2 meters each add 2.40, for 8.20 meters. That fits the 9 meter lot with 0.80 meters to spare.

The design is not finished just because it fits. The club still checks the budget for plywood and lumber, plans staggered seams and close stringers at the bottom, and confirms a guardrail on each platform. If many riders are brand new, Teresa might also lower the ramp to 0.9 meters. Engineering is the habit of testing each choice against the people who will use it.

words.d: a task with requirements and limits that is solved by planning, calculating and checking
a small halfpipe whose walls usually stop before vertical
a ramp with two facing transitions and usually a flat bottom between them

look.cite: Worked example: radius 1.8 m, height 1.2 m
look.prompt: If the flat bottom grew to 3.0 meters, would the ramp still fit in a 9 meter lot?

check.q: For h = 1.2 m and r = 1.8 m, what is the felt weight at the bottom?
The two curves are 1.70 m each, the flat bottom 2.4 m and each platform 1.2 m. What is the total length?
Why might the club lower the ramp to 0.9 meters?
choices: because many riders are brand new
check.why: A lower ramp means less speed, lower forces and shorter falls for new riders.

review.q: What sets how tight or mellow a transition is?
choices: the radius of the circle it is drawn from
review.why: A transition is an arc of a circle; a smaller radius makes a tighter curve.

review.q: A rider drops 2.0 m with no friction. What is the speed at the bottom?
Which energy change happens as a rider drops down a transition?
choices: potential energy turns into kinetic energy
kinetic energy turns into potential energy
review.why: Height energy (potential) becomes motion energy (kinetic) as the rider drops.

review.q: Where does a rider press up through the legs to pump?
choices: through the bottom of the curve
review.why: Pressing up where the ramp pushes back hardest, in the bottom of the curve, adds energy.

review.q: After a 1.5 m drop on a curve with a 1.5 m radius, how heavy does a rider feel at the bottom?
What is the coping used for?
choices: a grinding edge at the top of the transition
review.why: The coping is the edge at the top of the curve that riders grind and use to set up drop-ins.

review.q: Why are thin layers of plywood used for the riding surface?
choices: they bend to the curve without cracking
review.why: Thin plywood bends to the transition's curve; several layers give the needed strength.

review.q: What does a drop-in setup look like?
choices: front foot on the tail, back foot on the nose
tail on the coping, back foot on the tail, front foot over the front bolts
board on the flat bottom, feet on the ground
review.why: The tail sits on the coping with the back foot on it, and the front foot goes over the front bolts.
